intro: Every cook has a story like the potato salad in the sun or the pan that caught fire. Most of those stories end with a lesson learned the hard way: a cousin sick for two days, a scar on a wrist, a kitchen that smelled of smoke for a week. This unit is the lesson learned the easy way, before any of that happens. It is about the two kinds of harm a kitchen can do, the slow one from germs you cannot see and the fast one from heat, blades, electricity and fire.

In the first chapter you will learn the four habits that keep food from making people sick: clean, separate, cook and chill. You will meet the danger zone, 40 to 140 °F, and the two-hour rule. You will learn the safe temperatures for chicken, burgers, roasts and leftovers, how to use a food thermometer, and how to thaw and store food so bacteria never get their chance. Every number is the standard one from USDA and FDA guidance.

In the second chapter you will learn to prevent burns, cuts, falls, shocks and fires, and what to do in the first ten seconds when one happens anyway: the lid on the grease fire, PASS on the extinguisher, pressure on a cut, cool water on a burn, and when to call 911. You will finish with food allergies and how to read a label for the nine major allergens. By the end you will be ready to work in a kitchen where other people trust you with their food and their safety.
bigQuestion: How does a cook keep everyone in the kitchen, and everyone who eats from it, safe?

timeline.t: Louis Pasteur shows that heating a liquid kills the microbes that spoil it, the method now called pasteurization
Upton Sinclair's book about Chicago meatpacking plants shocks the nation and Congress passes the first federal meat inspection and food laws
Clarence Birdseye develops quick-freezing, and frozen food begins to reach home kitchens
Electric refrigerators replace iceboxes in many American homes, making a cold food chain possible
Food scientists working with the space program develop HACCP, a system for finding and controlling food safety hazards
A deadly E. coli outbreak from undercooked hamburgers leads to stricter rules and the 160 °F standard for ground beef
The Fight BAC! campaign launches with four words every cook now learns: clean, separate, cook, chill
A federal law requires packaged foods to name the major allergens in plain words
USDA sets whole cuts of pork at 145 °F with a three-minute rest; Congress passes the Food Safety Modernization Act
Sesame becomes the ninth major allergen that must be named on labels
You keep a thermometer in reach, a lid by the stove, and the four habits in your hands

words.d: 40 to 140 °F, the temperature range where bacteria grow fastest
perishable food can sit in the danger zone for two hours at most, one hour when the air is above 90 °F
the spread of bacteria from one food, surface, tool or hand to another
a probe that reads the temperature inside food; the only reliable way to know it is cooked safely
the lowest center temperature that kills harmful bacteria: poultry 165 °F, ground meat 160 °F, whole cuts and fish 145 °F
to treat a cleaned surface with heat or a chemical to kill the bacteria that washing leaves behind
food that spoils and can grow harmful bacteria if it is not kept cold or hot
a fire in cooking oil or fat; smother it with a lid or baking soda, never water
how to use a fire extinguisher: pull the pin, aim at the base, squeeze the handle, sweep side to side
a burn caused by hot liquid or steam; the most common kitchen injury
a severe, fast, whole-body allergic reaction that can close the airway; use epinephrine and call 911
the nine foods U.S. law requires on labels: milk, eggs, fish, shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans, sesame

test.q: What temperature range is the danger zone?
Cooked pasta sat on the counter in a 70 °F kitchen. When must it be thrown out?
test.why: The two-hour rule applies below 90 °F; above 90 °F the limit is one hour.

test.q: What is the safe minimum internal temperature for a hamburger?
test.why: Ground beef must reach 160 °F because grinding spreads surface bacteria through the meat.

test.q: What is the safe minimum internal temperature for chicken?
Where should raw chicken be stored in the refrigerator?
choices: In the crisper with the lettuce
test.why: Raw meat on the bottom shelf cannot drip onto ready-to-eat food.

choices: In the refrigerator on a plate
In hot water in the sink
test.why: Refrigerator thawing keeps the food below 40 °F the whole time.

test.q: How long should you scrub your hands with soap?
test.why: Twenty seconds is the standard, about two rounds of "Happy Birthday".

test.q: A cutting board was used for raw fish. Before slicing bread on it, what must happen?
choices: Wipe it with a dry towel
Wash it in hot soapy water and sanitize it, or use a different board
test.why: Raw fish leaves bacteria that a rinse does not remove; wash, sanitize or switch boards.

test.q: Leftovers are being reheated. What temperature should they reach?
test.why: Leftovers must reach 165 °F all the way through.

test.q: Oil in a pan catches fire. Which is the correct response?
choices: Turn off the burner and slide a lid over the pan
test.why: Cut the heat and smother the flames; water spreads burning oil.

test.q: In PASS, where do you aim the extinguisher?
choices: At the base of the fire
At the top of the flames
test.why: The fuel is at the base; aiming at the flames does nothing.

test.q: What is the first step for a burn from a hot pan?
choices: Hold it under cool running water
test.why: Cool tap water for at least ten minutes stops the heat from going deeper.

test.q: A cut is bleeding steadily. What is the first step?
choices: Press firmly with a clean cloth
Wrap it tightly with a rubber band
test.why: Steady pressure with a clean cloth stops bleeding.

test.q: Which situation means you should call 911?
choices: A grease fire that went out under the lid
A classmate who cannot breathe after eating
A first-degree burn on a finger
test.why: Trouble breathing, from choking or an allergic reaction, is a life-threatening emergency.

test.q: Which of these is one of the nine major food allergens?
test.why: Peanuts are one of the nine, along with milk, eggs, fish, shellfish, tree nuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame.

write.prompt: Write a safety plan for a cooking lab that will make chicken stir-fry and a fresh fruit salad. List the steps in order, from hand washing to putting the leftovers away, and after each step explain the rule or the number that makes it necessary. Include what to do if the oil catches fire and what to do if someone gets cut.
tips: Put the steps in the order they really happen: clean, then separate, then cook, then chill.
Name the tool for each step: the board for the chicken, the board for the fruit, the thermometer, the lid by the stove.
Write the exact number wherever there is one: 20 seconds, 165 °F, two hours, 40 °F.
For the fire and the cut, write what you do first, second and third, and what you must never do.
Read it back and ask: could a new student follow this without asking a question?

title: Kitchen Safety and Sanitation

chapters.title: Clean, Separate, Cook, Chill
chapters.bigQuestion: How do four habits keep food from making people sick?

story.title: The Potato Salad in the Sun
story.kicker: The family picnic had everything: a grill, a big cooler, and one bowl that nobody put away.
paragraphs: Marcus's aunt made the potato salad the night before. She boiled the potatoes, mixed in the mayonnaise, eggs and celery, covered the bowl and put it in the fridge. At the park the next day she set it on the picnic table at eleven in the morning, next to the buns and the chips. It was the first hot Saturday of June, and the thermometer on the shelter wall read 92 °F.

Uncle Ray ran the grill. He had a thermometer in his apron pocket and used it on every burger. "One-sixty," he said, showing Marcus the dial. "Ground beef has to hit 160. Chicken has to hit 165." He used one plate to carry raw patties out and a different clean plate to carry cooked ones back. Marcus thought that was a lot of fuss for a burger.

People ate lunch around noon. Then there was a softball game, then a second round of burgers around three. The potato salad was still on the table. The bowl was warm to the touch. Marcus's cousin Dee took a big spoonful. Marcus, who had been eating chips, did not.

By Sunday morning Dee and two other cousins were sick, with cramps and a fever. Marcus's aunt was upset. "I made it fresh," she said. "It was in the fridge all night." Uncle Ray shook his head. "It was not the fridge," he said. "It was the four hours on that table in the sun."

Later, Marcus looked up the rule. Food that should be cold cannot sit out more than two hours. When the air is above 90 °F, that drops to one hour. The salad had sat for four. Bacteria too small to see had been growing in it the whole afternoon, and nothing about the taste or smell gave them away.
story.think: Uncle Ray's burgers did not make anyone sick and the potato salad did. What did he do that nobody did for the salad?

lessons.title: Germs That Grow in Food
lessons.mainIdea: Bacteria you cannot see, taste or smell grow in food and cause most foodborne illness.
reading: Picture a container of leftover rice left on the counter overnight. In the morning it looks fine. It smells fine. It would taste fine. Yet a spoonful of it can hold millions of *bacteria*, living cells far too small to see, and some of them make poisons that cause vomiting and cramps. Food that makes you sick almost never looks spoiled. That is what makes it dangerous.

Bacteria need four things to multiply: food, moisture, warmth and time. Cooked rice, meat, eggs, dairy, cut fruit and cooked vegetables give them the first two. A warm room gives them the third. Every hour on the counter gives them the fourth. Under good conditions one cell can split into two about every twenty minutes, so a small number becomes a huge number in a few hours.

Sickness from food is called *foodborne illness*. Common causes include Salmonella, often found on raw poultry and eggs, and E. coli, linked to undercooked ground beef and unwashed produce. Symptoms may take hours or days to show up, so the meal that made you sick is often not the last one you ate.

You cannot see bacteria, so you cannot check food by looking. Instead, you control the four things they need. The rest of this chapter is four habits that do exactly that: clean, separate, cook and chill. Learn them once and you will use them for the rest of your life.

words.d: living cells too small to see; some kinds spoil food or cause illness
sickness caused by eating food that carries harmful germs or their poisons

look.title: The Rice on the Counter
look.text: A pot of rice was cooked at 6 p.m. and left on the stove with the lid on. At 8 a.m. it looks and smells exactly the same as it did last night. Someone says, "It's fine, it was covered." Think about the four things bacteria need and which ones the rice gave them overnight.
look.prompt: Explain why the lid did not protect the rice, and what should have happened at 8 p.m.

check.q: Which of these tells you food is safe to eat?
choices: It was kept cold and cooked to the right temperature
check.why: Harmful bacteria do not change the look, smell or taste of food. Only handling tells you it is safe.

check.q: What four things do bacteria need to multiply?
check.why: Bacteria need food, moisture, warmth and time. Food safety habits take away warmth and time.

check.q: Why is the last meal you ate not always the one that made you sick?
choices: Bacteria only grow in breakfast foods
Symptoms can take hours or days to appear
Sickness always comes from restaurant food
Only raw food can carry bacteria
check.why: Foodborne illness can show up hours or days later, so an earlier meal is often the cause.

lessons.title: The Danger Zone
lessons.mainIdea: Bacteria grow fastest between 40 and 140 °F, so keep cold food cold and hot food hot.
reading: Open a refrigerator and put a thermometer inside. It should read 40 °F or lower. Now think about a pot of soup on the stove, steaming at well over 140 °F. Between those two numbers is the *danger zone*: 40 to 140 °F. In that range, bacteria multiply quickly. Below it they slow down; above it they die off as food cooks.

Almost every room in a house sits inside the danger zone. A kitchen at 72 °F is right in the middle of it. That is why the counter is the worst place to keep food that needs to stay cold or hot. The fridge is below the zone. A hot oven or a warming tray is above it. The table at a picnic is inside it, and on a summer day it is deep inside it.

The fridge works only when it is truly cold. Set it at or below 40 °F and check it with a small fridge thermometer, because the dial on the door does not show degrees. The freezer should read 0 °F. Freezing does not kill bacteria; it stops them from growing. When frozen food thaws into the zone, they start growing again.

Keeping food out of the zone is the idea behind most of the rules you will learn. Chill leftovers fast. Cook meat all the way. Do not thaw on the counter. Each rule is one way of moving food through 40 to 140 °F as quickly as possible, or keeping it out entirely.

words.d: 40 to 140 °F, the temperature range where bacteria grow fastest
a small thermometer kept inside the refrigerator to check that it stays at or below 40 °F

look.title: Temperatures a Cook Should Know
look.cite: USDA and FDA food safety guidance
look.prompt: A kitchen at 72 °F sits inside the danger zone. Where would you keep a bowl of cut melon before lunch, and why?

check.q: What is the danger zone?
check.why: The danger zone is 40 to 140 °F, where bacteria multiply fastest.

check.q: What temperature should a refrigerator hold?
check.why: A refrigerator should be at or below 40 °F, just under the danger zone.

check.q: What does freezing do to bacteria in food?
choices: Stops them from growing until the food thaws
check.why: Freezing at 0 °F stops growth but does not kill bacteria; they resume growing when the food thaws.

lessons.title: The Two-Hour Rule
lessons.mainIdea: Perishable food may sit out two hours at most, or one hour when the air is above 90 °F.
reading: Think of the chicken on the counter after dinner. Dishes take a while, someone gets a phone call, and the chicken sits. The rule is simple: *perishable* food, meaning food that spoils, may stay in the danger zone for no more than two hours total. After that, throw it out. Do not taste it to check. Do not reheat it to fix it. Out.

Two hours is the limit for a normal room. When the air is above 90 °F, at a picnic, in a hot car, or on a porch in July, the limit drops to one hour. Bacteria grow faster in a hotter room, so they use up the safe time faster. The potato salad in the story sat for four hours at 92 °F, four times its limit.

The clock is a running total, not a fresh start. If the milk sat out for an hour at breakfast and an hour at lunch, its two hours are gone. To keep track, set a timer when food comes out of the fridge. A twenty-minute lunch is not a problem. A bowl left out through a whole movie is.

Perishable foods include meat, poultry, fish, eggs, dairy, cooked rice and pasta, cooked vegetables, cut fruit and anything made with them. Dry crackers, whole uncut fruit, bread and unopened cans are not. At a picnic, keep the perishables in a cooler with ice until the moment they are served, then put them back.

words.d: food that spoils and can grow harmful bacteria if it is not kept cold or hot
perishable food can sit in the danger zone for two hours at most, one hour when the air is above 90 °F

look.title: A Day of Small Sit-Outs
look.text: A carton of milk comes out at 7:00 a.m. and goes back at 7:40. It comes out again at 12:00 for lunch and goes back at 12:30. After school it sits on the counter from 3:30 to 4:45 while everyone does homework. Add up the minutes the milk spent in the danger zone.
look.prompt: Has the milk passed the two-hour rule? Show your total and say what you would do with the carton.

check.q: How long may cooked chicken sit out in a 72 °F kitchen?
check.why: The two-hour rule: perishable food gets two hours at most in the danger zone.

check.q: At a picnic where the air is 95 °F, how long may potato salad sit on the table?
check.why: Above 90 °F the limit drops to one hour because bacteria grow faster in heat.

check.q: Food sat out too long. What is the right move?
choices: Reheat it until it is steaming
Put it in the fridge right away
check.why: Reheating does not remove the poisons some bacteria make, and tasting cannot detect them. Throw it out.

lessons.title: Hands and Surfaces
lessons.mainIdea: Wash hands for twenty seconds with soap and water before, during and after handling food.
reading: Stand at the sink. Wet your hands with clean running water, turn the water off, and apply soap. Rub your palms, the backs of your hands, between your fingers and under your nails for a full *twenty seconds*, about the time it takes to hum "Happy Birthday" twice. Rinse under running water and dry with a clean towel or a paper towel. That is a hand wash. Anything shorter is a rinse.

Wash before you start cooking, after touching raw meat, poultry, fish or eggs, after using the bathroom, after touching your face, hair or phone, after handling trash, and after touching a pet. In a cooking lab that means washing several times in one class, and that is normal. Hand sanitizer is a backup for when there is no sink, but it does not remove grease or dirt the way soap does.

Surfaces need the same care. Before you begin, wipe the counter and cutting boards with hot soapy water. After raw meat touches a surface, wash it again with hot soapy water and then *sanitize* it, which means treating it to kill the bacteria that washing left behind. A common home sanitizer is a solution of a small amount of unscented bleach in water; follow the label.

Sponges and dish towels are a hidden problem. A damp sponge is warm, wet and full of food, all four things bacteria want. Use paper towels to clean up raw meat juices, change dish towels often, and let sponges dry out between uses or replace them. Tie back long hair, take off rings and bracelets, and wear an apron, so that you are not adding to the counter what you just cleaned off it.

words.d: the minimum time for scrubbing hands with soap, about two rounds of "Happy Birthday"
to treat a cleaned surface with heat or a chemical to kill the bacteria that washing leaves behind

look.title: Count the Hand Washes
look.text: In one lab a student washes hands, cuts raw chicken into strips, wipes her nose with the back of her hand, checks her phone for the recipe, tears lettuce for the salad, takes the trash bag out, and then plates the cooked chicken with her fingers.
look.prompt: Mark every moment she should have washed her hands again, and count them.

check.q: How long should you scrub with soap when washing your hands?
check.why: Twenty seconds of scrubbing with soap is the standard, about two rounds of "Happy Birthday".

check.q: You just cut raw chicken and now need to tear lettuce. What comes first?
choices: Wash hands with soap for twenty seconds
check.why: Raw poultry carries bacteria; a full soap-and-water wash is needed before touching ready-to-eat food.

check.q: Why is a damp kitchen sponge a problem?
choices: It stays warm, wet and full of food, so bacteria grow in it
check.why: A wet sponge gives bacteria food, moisture, warmth and time. Let it dry or replace it.

lessons.title: Produce and Dishes
lessons.mainIdea: Rinse produce under running water and wash dishes hot, soapy and in order.
reading: Take a head of lettuce and an apple. Even if you will peel the apple, rinse it first under cool running water and rub it with your hands. Otherwise the knife drags whatever is on the peel into the fruit. Pull the lettuce leaves apart and rinse each one, then dry them in a spinner or on a clean towel. Firm produce like potatoes and carrots can be scrubbed with a clean vegetable brush. Do not use soap; produce is not made to be eaten with soap on it.

Rinse produce right before you use it, not before you store it. Wet berries in the fridge grow mold. Cut the bruised or damaged spots away. Packaged salad marked "prewashed" or "ready to eat" does not need another rinse. Melons deserve special care: scrub the rind before cutting, because the knife carries anything on the outside straight through the sweet, wet inside.

Dishes get washed in a set order so the water stays clean as long as possible. Scrape food into the trash first. Fill the sink with hot, soapy water. Wash the least greasy items first: glasses and cups, then silverware, then plates and bowls, then pots and pans, and cutting boards that touched raw meat last of all. Rinse in hot water and let dishes air-dry in a rack, or dry them with a clean towel.

A dishwasher does the same job with hotter water than hands can stand, which is why it is a good place for cutting boards and knives that are dishwasher-safe. Cutting boards with deep knife grooves are hard to clean and should be replaced. Wooden boards should never soak; they crack, and cracks hold bacteria.

words.d: fresh fruits and vegetables
to let washed dishes dry in a rack instead of wiping them, so a towel cannot spread germs

look.title: Order the Dish Pile
look.text: In the sink after a lab: a greasy skillet, four water glasses, the cutting board used for raw chicken, six forks, two dinner plates with sauce on them, and a mixing bowl with a little batter left in it.
look.prompt: Put these in washing order, first to last, and say why the chicken board goes where it goes.

check.q: Why rinse an apple even if you plan to peel it?
choices: The knife carries dirt from the peel into the fruit
Water makes it easier to peel
Peeling does nothing, so rinsing is the only step
check.why: Whatever is on the peel travels on the blade into the flesh, so rinse first.

check.q: Which dishes are washed first in a sink of hot soapy water?
check.why: Wash the least greasy items first so the water stays clean: glasses, then silverware, plates, pots, and raw-meat boards last.

check.q: When should you rinse fresh berries?
choices: Before putting them in the fridge
check.why: Rinse produce just before use. Wet berries stored in the fridge grow mold faster.

lessons.title: Cross-Contamination
lessons.mainIdea: Cross-contamination moves bacteria from raw food to ready-to-eat food; separate keeps them apart.
reading: Picture a cutting board. Someone slices raw chicken on it, sets the chicken in the pan, and then slices tomatoes for a salad on the same board. The chicken is going to be cooked to 165 °F, so its bacteria will die. The tomatoes will not be cooked at all. Every germ the board picked up from the chicken now rides on the salad. This is *cross-contamination*: bacteria moving from one food, surface or hand to another.

Raw meat, poultry, fish and eggs are the usual sources. *Ready-to-eat* foods are the usual victims: salads, fruit, bread, cooked dishes, anything that will not be heated again before it is eaten. The rule is to keep the two groups apart at every stage: in the cart, in the fridge, on the counter, on the plate.

Cross-contamination happens through surfaces, through tools and through hands. A knife used on raw meat and then on cheese. A plate that carried raw burgers to the grill and then the cooked ones back. Tongs that flipped raw chicken and then served the cooked pieces. Hands that touched raw meat and then the fridge handle, the salt shaker and the bag of rolls.

The fix is a separate tool or a wash between uses. Two cutting boards, two plates, two sets of tongs, or one of each washed in hot soapy water in between. Never rinse raw poultry in the sink; the water splashes bacteria onto the counter, the faucet and the dishes nearby. Cooking kills the bacteria on the chicken anyway.

words.d: the spread of bacteria from one food, surface, tool or hand to another
food that will not be cooked before it is eaten, such as salad, fruit or bread

look.title: Find the Cross-Contamination
look.text: Dad cuts raw pork chops on the board, seasons them, and slides them into the oven. He rinses the board under the faucet, sets it back on the counter, and starts chopping cucumbers and peppers for a salad on it. He uses the same knife. Then he grabs the salad tongs from the drawer with the hand that seasoned the pork.
look.prompt: List every place bacteria from the pork could reach the salad, and say what would fix each one.

check.q: What is cross-contamination?
choices: Cooking two foods at the same time
Bacteria spreading from one food, tool or hand to another
Mixing ingredients in the wrong order
check.why: Cross-contamination is the spread of bacteria between foods, surfaces, tools and hands.

check.q: Raw chicken was cut on a board. What happens if you slice tomatoes on it next?
choices: The tomatoes will be fine because chicken bacteria only live in chicken
The tomatoes cook the bacteria away
The board's bacteria move onto tomatoes that will never be cooked
Nothing, if the board is plastic
check.why: The tomatoes are ready-to-eat and will not be cooked, so the chicken bacteria go straight to the plate.

check.q: Why should raw chicken not be rinsed in the sink?
choices: Splashing spreads bacteria around the sink and counter
check.why: Rinsing splashes bacteria onto surfaces; cooking to 165 °F kills them without the rinse.

lessons.title: Boards, Plates and Fridge Order
lessons.mainIdea: Use separate boards and plates for raw meat, and store raw meat on the bottom shelf.
reading: Many kitchens use color-coded cutting boards. One common scheme uses red for raw meat, yellow for raw poultry, blue for fish, and green for produce. Any scheme works as long as everyone in the kitchen uses the same one. At home, two boards are enough: one that only ever sees raw meat, poultry and fish, and one for everything else. Write it on the board if you have to.

Plates and tools follow the same idea. Carry raw burgers to the grill on one plate and bring the cooked burgers back on a clean one. Never put cooked food back on the plate that held it raw. Marinade that soaked raw meat cannot be served as a sauce unless it is boiled first; it is simpler to set some aside before it touches the meat.

The refrigerator has an order too. Raw meat, poultry and fish go on the bottom shelf, on a plate or in a container that catches drips. Ready-to-eat food goes above them. That way a leaking package of chicken drips onto the shelf below, not onto the strawberries. Eggs stay in their carton on a shelf, not in the door, because the door is the warmest spot.

At the store, the same rule applies. Put raw meat in the plastic bags the store provides, keep it apart from produce in the cart, and bag it separately at checkout. On the way home, it should be the last thing in the cart and the first thing in the fridge.

words.d: cutting boards in set colors so raw meat, poultry, fish and produce each get their own board
a seasoned liquid that raw meat soaks in; once it has touched raw meat it must be boiled or thrown out

look.title: Load the Fridge
look.text: Groceries on the counter: a package of raw chicken thighs, a bag of grapes, a carton of eggs, a tub of yogurt, a pound of raw ground beef, a bagged salad, and a package of cooked deli turkey. The fridge has a top shelf, a middle shelf, a bottom shelf, a crisper drawer and door shelves.
look.prompt: Say where each item goes and explain the one rule that decides the bottom shelf.

check.q: Where should raw chicken go in the refrigerator?
choices: On the bottom shelf in a container
check.why: Raw meat goes on the bottom shelf so any drips fall on nothing edible below.

check.q: Raw burgers went out to the grill on a plate. The cooked burgers should come back on what?
choices: The same plate, wiped with a napkin
A paper towel on the same plate
check.why: Cooked food never returns to a plate that held it raw; that is cross-contamination.

check.q: What can you do with marinade that soaked raw chicken if you want it as a sauce?
choices: Serve it as is; the vinegar kills germs
Chill it and serve it cold
Boil it first, or set some aside before it touches the chicken
check.why: Marinade from raw meat carries its bacteria; boiling kills them, or use a portion that never touched the meat.

lessons.title: The Food Thermometer
lessons.mainIdea: Only a thermometer in the thickest part of the food can tell you it has reached a safe temperature.
reading: Cut into a chicken thigh and the juices run clear, so it must be done, right? Not always. Color and juices are unreliable; some poultry stays pink at a safe temperature and some ground beef turns brown before it reaches one. The only way to know is a *food thermometer*. A digital instant-read thermometer costs about the price of a fast-food meal (example) and reads in a few seconds.

To use one, push the probe into the *thickest part* of the food, away from bone, fat and the pan. Bone heats faster than meat and gives a false high reading. For a thin burger, slide the probe in from the side so the tip reaches the middle. For a whole chicken, check the thickest part of the thigh and the thickest part of the breast. Wait for the numbers to stop moving.

Check the thermometer itself now and then. Fill a glass with crushed ice, top it with water, stir, and put the probe in without touching the sides. It should read 32 °F. If it does not, many thermometers have a small nut behind the dial or a reset button to adjust it. A thermometer that reads wrong is worse than none, because it makes you confident.

Wash the probe in hot soapy water after every use, especially between checking raw and cooked food. Pushing a probe that touched raw chicken into a cooked burger is cross-contamination with extra steps. Keep the thermometer where you can reach it; the one in the back of the drawer never gets used.

words.d: a probe that reads the temperature inside food; the only reliable way to know it is cooked safely
the deepest, densest spot in a piece of food, away from bone, where it cooks last

look.title: Where Does the Probe Go?
look.text: On the counter: a whole roasted chicken, a thin turkey burger in a skillet, a pork chop with the bone in, and a casserole dish of baked egg and cheese. Each needs a temperature check before it is served.
look.prompt: For each food, say exactly where you would put the thermometer probe and what mistake you are avoiding.

check.q: Where do you put the thermometer probe in a bone-in pork chop?
choices: In the thickest part of the meat, away from the bone
check.why: Bone gives a false high reading; the thickest part away from bone is the last spot to cook.

check.q: The juices from a chicken thigh run clear. What do you know?
choices: Nothing for sure; only a thermometer reading tells you
check.why: Color and juices are unreliable signs. Only a thermometer reading proves a safe temperature.

check.q: How do you check that a thermometer reads correctly?
choices: Hold it in the air and see if it matches the room
Compare it to the oven dial
Put it in ice water and look for 32 °F
check.why: A glass of ice water is 32 °F; a good thermometer reads that, and many can be adjusted if it does not.

lessons.title: Safe Minimum Temperatures
lessons.mainIdea: Every food has a safe minimum internal temperature; poultry is 165 °F, ground meat 160 °F, whole cuts and fish 145 °F.
reading: Here are the numbers, and they are worth memorizing. Poultry of every kind, whole, pieces or ground: 165 °F. Ground beef, pork, lamb and veal: 160 °F. Whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb and veal, such as steaks, chops and roasts: 145 °F, followed by a three-minute *rest* before cutting. Fish: 145 °F, or until the flesh is opaque and flakes with a fork. Egg dishes: 160 °F, and plain eggs cooked until the yolk and white are firm. Leftovers and casseroles reheated: 165 °F.

Why is ground meat higher than a steak? On a whole steak, bacteria live on the outside surface, which hits high heat first. Grinding mixes the outside all through the inside, so the center of a burger needs to reach 160 °F. A burger cooked to 145 °F is not safe just because a steak at 145 °F is. Poultry carries Salmonella so often that its number is the highest of all.

The three-minute rest for whole cuts is part of the cooking, not a suggestion. Take the roast out at 145 °F, cover it loosely with foil and leave it three minutes. The heat inside keeps working, and the juices settle so they do not run out when you slice. Reheating is easy to forget: leftovers must reach 165 °F all the way through, so stir them halfway and check the center, not the edge.

Microwaves cook unevenly, leaving cold spots where bacteria survive. Cover the food, stir or rotate it partway through, and let it stand a minute before checking the temperature. When a package says "cook until steaming hot," that is a rough guide. The thermometer is the real test, and 165 °F is the real target.

words.d: the lowest temperature at the center of a food that kills harmful bacteria
letting cooked meat sit a few minutes after it leaves the heat; whole cuts rest three minutes after 145 °F

look.title: Safe Minimum Internal Temperatures
rows: beef, pork, lamb, veal whole cuts (then rest 3 min)
look.cite: USDA safe minimum internal temperature chart
look.prompt: A burger and a steak both read 150 °F. One is safe and one is not. Which is which, and why?

check.q: What is the safe minimum internal temperature for a chicken breast?
check.why: All poultry, whole or ground, must reach 165 °F.

check.q: Why must a hamburger reach 160 °F when a steak only needs 145 °F?
choices: Grinding mixes surface bacteria all through the meat
Beef in burgers is lower quality
check.why: Grinding spreads the bacteria from the surface into the center, so the center needs 160 °F.

check.q: A pork roast reads 145 °F. What comes next?
choices: Let it rest three minutes before slicing
Put it in the fridge to stop the cooking
check.why: Whole cuts of pork are safe at 145 °F followed by a three-minute rest.

lessons.title: Thawing Safely
lessons.mainIdea: Thaw frozen food in the fridge, in cold water changed every 30 minutes, or in the microwave, never on the counter.
reading: A frozen chicken sits on the counter all day so it will be ready for dinner. By afternoon the outside has been in the danger zone for hours while the middle is still ice. That is the problem with counter thawing: the surface, where bacteria live, warms up first and stays warm longest. The counter is never a safe place to thaw meat, poultry or fish.

There are three safe ways. The first is the *refrigerator*. Put the frozen food on a plate on the bottom shelf and let the fridge do the work. It is slow, about a day for a package of chicken pieces and longer for a large roast, so plan ahead. Food thawed this way can stay in the fridge a day or two before cooking and can even be refrozen, though it may lose some quality.

The second is *cold water*. Seal the food in a leakproof bag, submerge it in cold tap water, and change the water every 30 minutes so it stays cold. A pound of meat takes about an hour; larger packages take longer. Cook the food right away once it thaws. The third is the microwave on its defrost setting, which warms parts of the food into the danger zone, so cook it immediately afterward.

You can also skip thawing. Frozen meat and poultry can go straight into the oven or onto the stove; it just takes about half again as long to cook, and you must still check it with a thermometer. What you cannot do is leave it in the sink, in hot water, or on the counter and hope.

words.d: the safest way to thaw: frozen food on a plate on the bottom shelf of the fridge, planned a day ahead
thawing sealed food under cold water changed every 30 minutes, then cooking it at once

look.title: Dinner Is in Four Hours
look.text: It is 2 p.m. A two-pound package of frozen ground beef needs to become tacos by 6 p.m. Someone suggests putting it in the sink in hot water. Someone else says to leave it on the counter. A third person says the microwave. A fourth says cold water in a bag.
look.prompt: Pick the safe options, reject the unsafe ones with the reason, and say what must happen right after each safe method.

check.q: Which is a safe way to thaw a frozen chicken?
choices: In the sink in hot water
In a bowl of cold water changed every 30 minutes
On the porch on a cool day
check.why: Cold-water thawing in a sealed bag with the water changed every 30 minutes keeps the surface out of the danger zone.

check.q: Why is counter thawing unsafe?
choices: The surface warms into the danger zone while the middle is still frozen
check.why: The outside of the food spends hours between 40 and 140 °F, where bacteria multiply.

check.q: Meat was thawed in the microwave. What must happen next?
choices: Put it in the fridge for later
check.why: Microwave thawing warms parts of the food into the danger zone, so it must be cooked immediately.

lessons.title: Cooling and Storing Leftovers
lessons.mainIdea: Get leftovers into the fridge within two hours, in shallow containers, and use them within about three to four days.
reading: Dinner is over and a big pot of chili is still on the stove. The old advice was to let it cool before it goes in the fridge, but a deep pot of hot chili can take many hours to cool, all of it in the danger zone. The rule now is the two-hour rule again: leftovers go into the fridge within two hours of cooking, and warm food is fine to put in.

The trick is *shallow containers*. Divide the chili into containers no more than about two inches deep so the cold reaches the middle quickly. Leave the lids loose until it stops steaming, then seal. Label each with the food and the date. Do not stack hot containers on top of one another; give them room for cold air to move.

Use refrigerated leftovers within about three to four days. If you will not eat them by then, freeze them; frozen food stays safe for a long time, though quality fades. Reheat leftovers to 165 °F, stirring so there are no cold spots. Reheat only what you will eat; food that has been reheated and cooled more than once has spent extra time in the danger zone.

A clean, cold fridge is the last piece. Wipe up spills right away. Do not pack it so full that air cannot move, because a crowded fridge has warm pockets. Keep a thermometer inside and check it: 40 °F or below. When you are not sure how old something is or whether it was handled safely, the rule is short and worth repeating: when in doubt, throw it out.

words.d: a storage container about two inches deep or less, so hot food cools quickly in the fridge
cooked food saved after a meal; chill within two hours, use within three to four days, reheat to 165 °F

look.title: Leftover Rules by the Numbers
rows: hours to get leftovers into the fridge
depth of a cooling container, at most (inches)
days to use refrigerated leftovers, about
look.cite: USDA leftovers and food safety guidance
look.prompt: A pot of soup is put in the fridge whole, four inches deep, five hours after dinner. Which numbers were broken?

check.q: A big pot of chili is done at 6 p.m. By when must it be in the fridge?
choices: The next morning, once it is fully cool
check.why: The two-hour rule applies to leftovers; from 6 p.m. that means 8 p.m.

check.q: Why divide hot food into shallow containers?
choices: So the cold reaches the middle quickly
check.why: Shallow containers, about two inches deep, let food cool through quickly instead of sitting in the danger zone.

check.q: To what temperature should leftovers be reheated?
check.why: Reheated leftovers must reach 165 °F all the way through.

review.q: Which range is the danger zone?
Perishable food sat out at a picnic where the air was 88 °F. What is its limit?
review.why: At 88 °F the air is below 90 °F, so the normal two-hour limit applies.

review.q: What is the safe minimum internal temperature for ground turkey?
review.why: Ground turkey is poultry, and all poultry must reach 165 °F.

review.q: Which fridge arrangement follows the separate rule?
choices: Raw chicken on the bottom shelf in a container, salad above it
Raw chicken on the top shelf, salad below it
Raw chicken in the crisper drawer with the lettuce
review.why: Raw meat goes on the bottom shelf so drips cannot land on ready-to-eat food.

review.q: A cook rinses raw chicken in the sink before cooking. What is the problem?
choices: Splashing spreads bacteria over the sink and counter
The rinse washes away the seasoning
review.why: Rinsing raw poultry splashes bacteria around; cooking to 165 °F kills them without rinsing.

review.q: A steak reads 145 °F on the thermometer. What is the next step?
choices: Rest it three minutes, then serve
review.why: Whole cuts of beef are safe at 145 °F with a three-minute rest.

review.q: Which thawing method is NOT safe?
choices: In the refrigerator on a plate
In cold water changed every 30 minutes
In the microwave, then cooked at once
On the counter for the afternoon
review.why: Counter thawing leaves the surface in the danger zone for hours.

review.q: Leftover rice cooked at 6 p.m. should be in the fridge by when, and in what kind of container?
choices: Whenever it is cold, in a deep bowl
review.why: Leftovers go in within two hours in shallow containers so they cool through quickly.

chapters.title: Preventing Kitchen Accidents
chapters.bigQuestion: What do you do in the first ten seconds of a kitchen emergency, and how do you keep it from happening at all?

story.title: The Pan That Caught Fire
story.kicker: It was the third week of cooking lab, the oil was too hot, and somebody reached for a cup of water.
paragraphs: Station four was frying plantains. Jayden had the skillet on high with a quarter inch of oil in it, and he turned around to find the spatula. When he turned back, the oil was smoking, then it was not smoke anymore. Flames rose off the surface of the oil in a low, orange sheet. Somebody screamed. Somebody else laughed, then stopped laughing.

Lena at the next station grabbed a measuring cup, filled it at the sink and started toward the stove. Ms. Okafor's voice cut through the room. "No water. Lena, put it down." Lena froze with the cup in her hand. Water on burning oil does not put it out. It flashes to steam under the oil and throws the burning grease into the air.

Ms. Okafor was already at the stove. She reached past the pan, not over it, and turned the burner off. Then she took the skillet's lid from the hook on the wall, held it like a shield with the oven mitt, and slid it over the pan from the near edge. The flames went out under the lid the moment the air was gone. She left the lid on and the pan where it was.

"Nobody touches that pan for twenty minutes," she said. "If you lift the lid now, the air goes back in and it can light again." She pointed at the red extinguisher by the door. "That was next, if the lid had not worked. And 911 after that, from the hallway, not from in here."

Jayden was shaking. Nothing was burned but a little oil and his pride. That afternoon the class did not cook. They walked through what had happened, second by second: the oil left on high, the turn away from the stove, the water, the lid. By the end of the period every student could say the three things you do for a grease fire, in order, without looking at the board.
story.think: Ms. Okafor did three things in order: burner off, lid on, leave it alone. What would have gone wrong if she had skipped any one of them?

lessons.title: Burns and Scalds
lessons.mainIdea: Most kitchen burns come from steam, hot handles and splashing oil, and every one of them is preventable.
reading: Lift the lid off a pot of boiling pasta and tilt it toward you. The steam that rolls out is over 212 °F and it burns skin instantly. That is a *scald*, a burn from hot liquid or steam, and it is the most common kitchen injury. Always lift a lid away from your face, so the steam escapes on the far side. Open the oven door partway and wait a second before leaning in.

Handles are the next problem. A pot handle sticking out over the front of the stove is a handle someone will hit with an elbow. Turn every handle toward the back or the side, over the counter, not over another burner. A metal handle on a skillet that has been in the oven is as hot as the oven. Leave the mitt on it, or drape a towel over it, so the next person knows.

Use dry *oven mitts* or pot holders, never a wet towel; water in the cloth turns to steam against your hand. Set hot pans on a trivet or a cooling rack, not on the counter or on a plastic cutting board. Pull the oven rack out to reach a dish instead of reaching into the oven. When you add food to hot oil, lower it in with tongs so it does not splash.

Microwaves cause their own burns. A bowl can be cool while the food inside is far hotter, and liquids heated too long can boil up suddenly when moved. Let food stand a minute, stir it, and take it out with a mitt. Keep small children away from the stove entirely, and keep the cords of kettles and slow cookers pushed back where nobody can pull them.

words.d: a burn caused by hot liquid or steam
a thick, dry glove for holding hot pans; a wet one turns to steam and burns
a heatproof stand that a hot pot rests on so it does not burn the counter

look.title: Spot the Burn Waiting to Happen
look.text: A stove with four burners. Front left: a pot of boiling water with the handle pointing straight out into the room. Back right: a skillet that just came out of a 425 °F oven, sitting with its bare metal handle facing forward. A damp dish towel hangs over the oven door. A student is about to lift the pasta pot's lid straight up toward her face.
look.prompt: Name every burn hazard in this scene and say what you would change about each one.

check.q: How should you lift the lid off a boiling pot?
choices: Tilted away from your face so the steam goes the other way
Tilted toward you so you can see inside
With a wet towel for grip
check.why: Steam escapes on the side the lid opens; tilting it away keeps the scald off your face.

check.q: Why should you never use a wet towel to pick up a hot pan?
choices: The water turns to steam and burns through to your hand
check.why: Water in the cloth becomes steam against your skin. Use a dry mitt or pot holder.

check.q: Which way should pot handles point on the stove?
choices: Toward the back or side, over the counter
Straight out front for easy grabbing
It does not matter on an electric stove
check.why: Handles turned in cannot be knocked by an elbow or grabbed by a child.

lessons.title: Cuts and Falls
lessons.mainIdea: A sharp knife, a steady board and a dry floor prevent most cuts and falls.
reading: A dull knife slides off a tomato skin and into a finger. A sharp knife bites in where you point it. That is why a *sharp knife* is the safer one: it takes less force, so it does not slip. Keep the board from sliding by laying a damp towel under it. Curl the fingers of your holding hand into a claw so the knuckles, not the fingertips, face the blade.

Cut on a board, never in your hand. Cut away from your body. Never try to catch a falling knife; step back and let it land. Carry a knife at your side, point down, blade toward the back, and tell people "knife behind you" when you pass. Never leave a knife in a sink of soapy water where a hand will find it by accident. Wash it, dry it and put it away.

Other sharp things hide in the kitchen: the lid of an opened can, the blade of a blender or food processor, a box grater, a broken glass. Sweep broken glass with a broom, not your fingers, and wrap it in newspaper before it goes in the trash. Unplug a blender before you reach into it, and wash its blade separately, holding the base.

Falls happen on wet floors and from chairs used as ladders. Wipe up every spill the moment it happens, water or grease, and say "spill" so nobody steps in it. Use a step stool with a handrail to reach a high shelf, not a chair and not the counter. Keep cabinet doors and drawers closed. Tie shoelaces, and wear closed-toe shoes in a lab, because a dropped knife or a splash of oil lands on feet.

words.d: the safer knife: it needs less force, so it does not slip off food and into a hand
curling the fingers of the holding hand so the knuckles guide the blade and fingertips stay back

look.title: Two Minutes in a Busy Kitchen
look.text: A cook drops a knife and grabs for it. Another leaves a paring knife in the dishwater. A third stands on a swivel chair to reach the colander. A puddle of oil from a spilled bottle sits by the stove. Someone reaches into the blender to loosen a stuck strawberry while it is still plugged in.
look.prompt: Rank these from most to least dangerous, and give the safe move for each.

check.q: A knife slips off the counter and falls. What do you do?
choices: Step back and let it fall
check.why: Never catch a falling knife; step back and pick it up once it lands.

check.q: Why is a dull knife more dangerous than a sharp one?
choices: It needs more force and slips off food
check.why: A dull blade requires force and skids off the food; a sharp one cuts where it is aimed.

check.q: You need a bowl from the top shelf. What do you stand on?
choices: A step stool with a handrail
check.why: A step stool is made for climbing; chairs and counters cause falls.

lessons.title: Electric Shock and Cords
lessons.mainIdea: Water and electricity never mix; keep cords dry, short and unplugged before you reach in.
reading: A toaster with a slice stuck in it, and a fork in someone's hand. The metal fork touches the heating element and the current runs up the fork into the person. Always *unplug* an appliance before you reach into it, fix it, or clean it. Then use wooden tongs for the toaster, and let it cool.

Water carries electricity. Never plug in or unplug anything with wet hands, and never use an appliance near a full sink. If a plugged-in appliance falls into water, do not reach for it. Unplug it first, or turn off the circuit breaker if you cannot reach the plug safely. Kitchens have special outlets called *GFCI* outlets, with test and reset buttons, that shut off power in a fraction of a second when they sense a fault. Test them monthly.

Cords cause accidents in two ways. A cord that hangs over the counter edge is a cord a child or a dog can pull, bringing a kettle of boiling water down with it. A cord that lies across a hot burner melts, and a melted cord can shock or start a fire. Route cords along the back of the counter. Pull plugs out by the plug, not by the cord, so the wires inside stay attached.

Look at cords before you use them. Frayed insulation, exposed wire, a plug that is warm or scorched, or an appliance that buzzes, smells hot or sparks all mean stop, unplug and tell an adult. Do not overload one outlet with a power strip full of high-heat appliances; a toaster oven, a kettle and a microwave together can trip a breaker or heat the wiring.

words.d: to disconnect an appliance from the outlet; do it before reaching inside or cleaning it
a ground-fault outlet with test and reset buttons that cuts power fast when it senses a fault; required near water
the switch in the electrical panel that shuts off power to part of the house

look.title: The Toast Is Stuck
look.text: A slice of bread is jammed in the toaster and it is still plugged in and warm. On the counter beside it are a metal fork, a pair of wooden tongs, and a glass of water. The cord runs across the front of the counter and dangles near the floor.
look.prompt: Write the steps to get the toast out safely, in order, and then fix what is wrong with the cord.

check.q: Toast is stuck in the toaster. What is the first step?
choices: Poke it out with a fork
check.why: Unplug before reaching into any appliance; metal in a live toaster can shock you.

check.q: A plugged-in hand mixer falls into a sink of water. What do you do?
choices: Grab it fast before it shorts out
Unplug it or shut off the breaker before touching it
Lift it out with a towel
check.why: Water carries current. Cut the power first, then retrieve the appliance.

check.q: What does a GFCI outlet do?
choices: Cuts power in a fraction of a second when it senses a fault
Stops the toaster from burning bread
check.why: GFCI outlets protect against shock near water by shutting off power almost instantly.

lessons.title: The Grease Fire
lessons.mainIdea: For a grease fire: turn off the heat, slide a lid over the pan, and never use water.
reading: Oil in a pan can get hot enough to light itself. When it does, you have seconds, and the first move is the burner: turn it *off*. The second move is to cut off the air. Take a metal lid or a baking sheet, hold it with a mitt, and slide it over the pan from the near edge, keeping your arm out from over the flames. No air, no fire. Leave the lid on until the pan is completely cool.

If there is no lid, pour *baking soda* on a small fire. A lot of it, not a pinch. Baking soda releases carbon dioxide when heated, which smothers the flames. Salt also works by smothering. Never use flour, sugar or baking mix; fine powders can ignite in the air and turn a small fire into a fireball.

Never, ever use *water*. Water is heavier than oil, so it sinks under the burning grease, boils instantly and blasts flaming oil out of the pan and across the kitchen. Do not carry the burning pan to the sink or outside either; the flames blow back on you and the oil sloshes. The pan stays where it is.

If the lid and the baking soda do not work, or if the fire has spread past the pan to a cabinet or a curtain, it is no longer a pan fire. Get everyone out, close the door behind you and call 911 from outside. A kitchen fire extinguisher is for a fire still small enough to face; the next lesson shows how to use one. Prevention is easier: never leave hot oil unattended, heat oil on medium, and keep a lid within reach every time you fry.

words.d: a fire in cooking oil or fat; smother it with a lid or baking soda, never water
sodium bicarbonate; releases carbon dioxide when heated and can smother a small grease fire
to put out a fire by cutting off its air

look.title: Order the Grease-Fire Steps
look.text: Here are six actions in scrambled order: slide a lid over the pan; turn off the burner; call 911 from outside if it spreads; pour a cup of water on it; leave the lid on until the pan is cool; carry the pan to the sink. Two of them are things you must never do.
look.prompt: Write the correct steps in order, cross out the two forbidden ones, and explain what each forbidden one would cause.

check.q: Oil in a skillet catches fire. What is the first step?
choices: Carry the pan to the sink
check.why: Cut the heat first, then smother the flames with a lid.

check.q: Why does water make a grease fire worse?
choices: It cools the oil too fast
It sinks under the oil, boils and throws burning grease into the air
It puts out the pilot light
check.why: Water is heavier than oil; it flashes to steam under the grease and sprays flaming oil out of the pan.

check.q: Which powder can smother a small grease fire?
check.why: Baking soda releases carbon dioxide and smothers flames. Flour and sugar can ignite.

lessons.title: PASS and the Extinguisher
lessons.mainIdea: Use a fire extinguisher with PASS: pull, aim at the base, squeeze, sweep, with your back to the exit.
reading: Find the *fire extinguisher* in your kitchen or lab right now, before you need it. It should be near an exit, not behind the stove where the fire would be. Read the label: a home kitchen extinguisher is usually rated ABC, meaning it works on ordinary materials (A), flammable liquids like grease (B) and electrical fires (C). Restaurant kitchens use a Class K extinguisher made for deep fryers.

The steps spell *PASS*. Pull the pin at the top of the handle. Aim the nozzle at the base of the fire, not the flames, because the fuel is at the bottom. Squeeze the handle. Sweep the nozzle side to side across the base until the fire is out. Stand about six to eight feet back to start and move closer as the fire dies down.

Before you use it, make two decisions. Is the fire small, meaning no bigger than a wastebasket, and not spreading? And is the exit behind you, so you can back out if it grows? If either answer is no, do not fight the fire. Leave, close the door, and call 911. An extinguisher empties in seconds; it gets one try.

Afterward, watch the spot for a few minutes in case it lights again, and open windows to clear the powder. Even a partly used extinguisher must be replaced or recharged. Check the gauge on any extinguisher once a month: the needle should sit in the green. Install a smoke alarm near the kitchen and test it monthly too; most kitchen fires start on the stove, and most are found early by a working alarm.

words.d: a pressurized canister that sprays a fire-smothering agent; kitchen models are rated ABC or K
pull the pin, aim at the base, squeeze the handle, sweep side to side
the bottom of the flames where the fuel is; aiming at the flames themselves does nothing

look.title: Fight or Flee?
look.text: Three scenes. One: a small fire in a toaster, contained, with the door to the hallway right behind you. Two: flames climbing the curtain above the stove and reaching the cabinets, with the only door on the far side of the stove. Three: a trash can fire the size of a basketball in the corner near the exit.
look.prompt: For each scene, say whether you would use the extinguisher or leave and call 911, and name the two questions that decide it.

check.q: What does the A in PASS stand for?
choices: Aim at the base of the fire
check.why: Aim the nozzle at the base of the fire, where the fuel is, not at the flames.

check.q: Where should you stand when using an extinguisher?
choices: Between the fire and the exit, with your back to the exit
In the doorway of another room
check.why: Keep the exit behind you so you can back out if the fire grows.

check.q: Flames have spread from the pan to the cabinets above the stove. What do you do?
choices: Use the extinguisher from up close
Get out, close the door and call 911
check.why: A spreading fire is too big for an extinguisher; leave, close the door and call 911.

lessons.title: Oven, Range and Appliances
lessons.mainIdea: Never leave the stove unattended, keep the area clear, and know how to shut off every appliance.
reading: The most common cause of kitchen fires is a stove left alone. Oil heats faster than people expect, a towel slides onto a burner, a pot boils dry. The rule is simple: if you are frying, grilling or broiling, stay in the kitchen. If you leave the room, turn the burner off. Set a timer for anything simmering or baking so it cannot be forgotten.

Keep the *cook zone* clear. Nothing that can burn within three feet of the stovetop: no towels, paper, oven mitts, plastic bags, wooden spoons or cereal boxes. Wear short or rolled sleeves. Clean grease off the stovetop and out of the range hood filter, because old grease is fuel. On a gas stove, if you smell gas and the burner did not light, turn the knob off, do not light anything, and open a window.

Ovens have their own rules. Open the door and stand to the side for a second before leaning in. If something catches fire inside the oven, keep the door closed and turn the oven off; the fire will smother itself. The same goes for a fire inside a microwave: keep the door shut, turn it off, unplug it. Do not put metal in the microwave, and do not run it empty.

Small *appliances* like toaster ovens, air fryers, slow cookers and electric kettles get hot on the outside too. Give them space from the wall and from each other, unplug them when they are not in use, and never wrap the cord around a hot unit. Know where the stove knobs are without looking, and where the breaker panel is. In an emergency, you shut things off by feel and by memory, not by reading.

words.d: left with nobody watching; an unattended stove is the top cause of kitchen fires
the area within three feet of the stovetop, kept clear of anything that can burn
the vent above the stove; its filter collects grease that must be cleaned out

look.title: A Fire in the Oven
look.text: A cheese-topped casserole bubbles over, and the drips on the oven floor catch fire. Through the oven window you can see flames. Your first instinct is to open the door and grab the dish.
look.prompt: Explain why opening the door is the wrong move and write the three things you would do instead.

check.q: What is the most common cause of kitchen fires?
check.why: Most kitchen fires begin on a stove nobody is watching.

check.q: Something catches fire inside the oven. What should you do?
choices: Open the door and pull it out
Keep the door closed and turn the oven off
Fan the oven with a towel
check.why: A closed oven starves the fire of air; opening the door feeds it oxygen.

check.q: A gas burner clicks but does not light and you smell gas. What is right?
choices: Turn the knob off and open a window
check.why: Turn off the gas, do not light anything, and let fresh air clear the room.

lessons.title: Treating a Cut
lessons.mainIdea: For a cut: wash your hands, press with a clean cloth, rinse, bandage, and get help if it will not stop bleeding.
reading: The knife slips and there is blood on the board. First, stop and put the knife down. Wash your hands if you can, then press a clean cloth or paper towel firmly on the cut. Steady *pressure* is what stops bleeding. Hold it, do not peek every few seconds, and raise the hand above the heart if you can. Most small cuts stop within a few minutes.

Once the bleeding slows, rinse the cut under clean running water to wash out anything in it. Do not use hydrogen peroxide or alcohol inside the wound; they damage the tissue. Pat it dry with a clean cloth, apply a thin layer of antibiotic ointment if you have it, and cover it with a clean *bandage*. In a food lab, cover the bandage with a disposable glove before touching food again.

Some cuts need a doctor. Get help if the bleeding does not stop after steady pressure, if the cut is deep or gaping, if it is on the face or over a joint, if something is stuck in it, or if it came from a dirty or rusty object. Bleeding that spurts or soaks through a cloth is an emergency; call 911 and keep pressing.

The food on the board is done. Anything the blood touched goes in the trash, and the board, the knife and the counter get washed and sanitized before work continues. Tell the teacher or an adult about every cut, even a small one. Write it down if the lab keeps an injury log; the point is not blame but finding the pattern that caused it.

words.d: pressing firmly on a wound with a clean cloth to stop bleeding; the first step for any cut
a clean covering that protects a wound; in a kitchen, cover it with a glove before touching food

look.title: The Slip on the Onion
look.text: A student cuts the side of a finger while slicing an onion. The cut bleeds steadily but does not spurt. The student's first move is to hold it under the faucet, and then to pour hydrogen peroxide on it from the first aid kit.
look.prompt: Rewrite what the student did into the correct order of steps, and say which of the two moves was a mistake and why.

check.q: What is the first thing to do for a bleeding cut?
choices: Press a clean cloth firmly on it
Run cold water on it for ten minutes
Wrap it in a rubber band
check.why: Firm, steady pressure with a clean cloth stops bleeding.

check.q: When does a cut need emergency help?
choices: When it is on a finger
When it will not stop bleeding or is spurting
When it happened on a cutting board
check.why: Bleeding that spurts or does not stop with pressure is an emergency; call 911.

check.q: You have bandaged a cut and want to keep cooking. What goes over the bandage?
check.why: A glove over the bandage keeps blood and bandage out of the food.

lessons.title: Treating a Burn
lessons.mainIdea: Cool a burn under cool running water, cover it loosely, and never put ice, butter or ointment on it.
reading: A hand brushes the oven rack. The skin turns red and starts to sting. Get it under *cool running water* right away, from the tap, not ice cold, and keep it there for at least ten minutes if you can. Cooling stops the heat from going deeper into the skin. Take off rings or watches near the burn before it swells.

Do not use ice; it damages burned skin further. Do not put on butter, oil, toothpaste or grease, which trap the heat in and can cause infection. After cooling, cover the burn loosely with a clean, dry cloth or a sterile non-stick dressing. Do not pop a *blister*; the skin over it protects the raw layer underneath.

Burns are graded by depth. A first-degree burn is red and painful, like a mild sunburn. A second-degree burn blisters. A third-degree burn looks white, leathery or charred and may not hurt at all because the nerves are damaged. Any burn larger than the palm of your hand, any burn on the face, hands, feet or a joint, and any third-degree burn needs a doctor, and a large or deep burn means 911.

For a scald from hot liquid soaked into clothing, get the clothing off fast unless it is stuck to the skin; the wet cloth keeps burning. For a grease splash, same rule: cool water, then cover. Report every burn to the teacher. Then look at what caused it, because the fix for a burn is almost always something you can change next time: a mitt, a handle turned in, a lid tilted the other way.

words.d: the first treatment for a burn: tap water, not ice, run over the burn for at least ten minutes
a fluid-filled bubble over a burn; leave it unbroken because it protects the skin beneath
a burn through all layers of skin, white or charred and often painless; always an emergency

look.title: Burn Depths and What They Look Like
rows: first-degree: red, painful, no blister (layers of skin affected)
third-degree: white or charred, may be painless (layers, all the way through)
minutes under cool running water, at least
look.prompt: A burn from a steam scald has blistered. What degree is it, and what do you do and not do about the blister?

check.q: What is the first treatment for a burn?
check.why: Cool tap water for at least ten minutes stops the heat from going deeper. Ice damages the skin.

check.q: A burn has formed a blister. What do you do with it?
choices: Pop it with a clean pin
Leave it alone and cover loosely
check.why: The blister protects the raw skin under it; leave it intact.

check.q: A burn looks white and leathery and does not hurt. What does that mean?
choices: It is a third-degree burn and needs emergency care
check.why: No pain with white or charred skin means the nerves are damaged; that is a third-degree burn.

lessons.title: When to Call 911
lessons.mainIdea: Call 911 for fire, trouble breathing, heavy bleeding, a large burn, or anyone unconscious; know the address before you dial.
reading: The hardest part of an emergency is deciding it is one. Call *911* when a fire is not out after the lid, when someone cannot breathe or is choking and cannot cough, when bleeding spurts or soaks through cloth, when a burn is large or deep, when someone is unconscious, or when someone has swallowed a chemical. If you are not sure, call. The dispatcher would rather answer a call that was not needed than miss one that was.

Know your *address* before the emergency. In a school lab that means the school name, the street, and the room number. On the phone, say where you are first, then what happened. Stay on the line; the dispatcher will tell you what to do while help is coming. Speak slowly. Send someone to the door to wave the ambulance in.

For choking, the sign is a person who cannot speak, cough or breathe and may grab their throat. If they can cough, let them cough. If they cannot, call 911 and, if you are trained, give back blows and abdominal thrusts. First-aid training from the Red Cross or a similar group teaches this and CPR in one afternoon, and every kitchen worker should have it.

Keep a list where everyone can see it: 911, the Poison Control number, the school office or a parent's number, and the address. Keep the first aid kit stocked and in a marked spot. Practice matters. A class that has walked through "what would we do if" acts in seconds, and seconds are what a kitchen emergency gives you.

words.d: the emergency number in the United States for fire, police and ambulance
the exact location you give the dispatcher first: building, street and room
the person who answers 911, sends help and gives instructions while it comes

look.title: Call or Handle It?
look.text: Five moments: a paper cut on a thumb; a classmate who has gone quiet and is grabbing his throat after a bite of hot dog; a grease fire that went out under the lid; a burn the size of a quarter on a forearm; a student who fainted and is not waking up.
look.prompt: Sort them into call 911 now, handle with first aid, and handle then tell an adult. Say what you would tell the dispatcher for the 911 ones.

check.q: Which situation means call 911 right away?
choices: A person who is choking and cannot cough or speak
A small cut that stopped bleeding
A grease fire that went out under the lid
A first-degree burn on a fingertip
check.why: Someone who cannot breathe, cough or speak needs emergency help immediately.

check.q: What do you tell the dispatcher first?
check.why: Location comes first so help can be sent even if the call is cut off.

check.q: A classmate is coughing hard after a bite of food went down wrong. What do you do?
choices: Slap her on the back hard
Let her keep coughing and watch closely
check.why: If a person can cough, air is moving; let them cough and act only if they cannot.

lessons.title: The Major Allergens
lessons.mainIdea: Nine foods cause most serious allergic reactions, and even a trace can be dangerous to someone allergic.
reading: A friend at your table takes a bite of a cookie and, within minutes, her lips swell and her breathing sounds tight. That is a *food allergy*: the body's defense system treats a harmless food as an attacker. Reactions range from hives and an itchy mouth to *anaphylaxis*, a whole-body reaction that closes the airway and drops blood pressure. Anaphylaxis can kill within minutes.

In the United States, nine foods are the *major allergens* named by law: milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish such as shrimp and crab, tree nuts such as almonds and walnuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame. Sesame was added to the list in 2023. These nine cause most serious reactions, though a person can be allergic to almost anything.

The amount does not have to be large. For some people, a knife that spread peanut butter and was wiped on a towel carries enough peanut to cause a reaction. That is why allergens are handled like raw chicken: separate tools, separate boards, hands washed with soap and water, and surfaces scrubbed. Hand sanitizer does not remove allergen proteins; soap and water do.

Many people with severe allergies carry an *epinephrine auto-injector*, a pen-shaped device that injects a dose of medicine into the thigh. If someone is having a serious reaction, help them use it, then call 911, because the medicine wears off and a second reaction can follow. Ask about allergies before you cook for anyone, and take the answer seriously. "A little won't hurt" is not true.

words.d: an immune reaction to a food protein; can range from hives to anaphylaxis
a severe, fast, whole-body allergic reaction that can close the airway; call 911
the nine foods named by U.S. law: milk, eggs, fish, shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans, sesame
a pen-shaped device that injects emergency allergy medicine into the thigh

look.title: The Peanut Butter Knife
look.text: One student spreads peanut butter on crackers, wipes the knife with the shared dish towel, and rinses the knife under water. A second student, who is allergic to peanuts, uses that towel to dry her hands, then uses the same knife to cut an apple.
look.prompt: Trace the peanut protein from the jar to the second student, and name each step where soap, a separate tool or a fresh towel would have stopped it.

check.q: How many major food allergens are named by U.S. law?
check.why: Nine: milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame.

check.q: Someone is having anaphylaxis and has an epinephrine auto-injector. What is the order?
choices: Wait to see if it gets worse, then call
Help with the auto-injector, then call 911
Give water and have them lie down
check.why: Epinephrine first, then 911, because the medicine can wear off and the reaction can return.

check.q: Why is hand sanitizer not enough after handling peanuts?
choices: It kills bacteria but does not remove allergen proteins
check.why: Allergen proteins must be washed away with soap and water; sanitizer leaves them on the skin.

lessons.title: Reading the Label for Allergens
lessons.mainIdea: Check the ingredient list and the Contains line every time, because recipes change.
reading: Pick up a package of granola bars and turn it over. Under the *ingredient list* there is often a line in bold: "Contains: milk, peanuts, soy." U.S. law requires packaged foods to name any of the nine major allergens in plain words, either in the ingredient list or in a *Contains statement* right below it. "Whey" must be labeled as milk; "albumin" as egg.

Some labels add a line such as "May contain tree nuts" or "Made in a facility that also processes peanuts." These *advisory statements* are voluntary and mean the food could have picked up traces on shared equipment. For someone with a severe allergy, that is a reason to skip the product. Never assume; a food with no advisory line is not promised to be trace-free.

Read the label every single time, even on a food you have bought a hundred times. Companies change recipes, and the new version can add an allergen without changing the front of the box. Read it at the store, and read it again before you cook. In a lab, keep the packages until the food is served so the label can be checked if someone asks.

Allergens hide in unexpected places. Soy in bread and chocolate, milk in deli meat, egg in some pasta and salad dressings, wheat in soy sauce, fish in Worcestershire sauce, peanuts in some chili and mole sauces. If a dish is for someone with an allergy and you cannot read a label for every ingredient, do not serve it. Say so plainly. A missed meal is nothing compared to a missed allergen.

words.d: the list on a package of everything in the food, in order from most to least
the bold line under the ingredients that names any major allergens in the food
a voluntary warning such as "may contain" that the food could carry traces from shared equipment

look.title: Read This Label
look.text: Ingredients: whole grain oats, sugar, sunflower oil, honey, rice flour, whey, natural flavor, soy lecithin, salt. Contains: milk, soy. May contain peanuts and tree nuts. A classmate with a tree-nut allergy asks if she can have one. Another classmate, allergic to milk, says he does not see "milk" in the ingredients so it must be fine.
look.prompt: Answer both classmates using the label, and explain which word in the ingredient list the second classmate missed.

check.q: Where does U.S. law require major allergens to be named?
choices: Only on the front of the package
In the ingredient list or a Contains statement below it
check.why: Packaged foods must name the nine major allergens in plain words in the ingredients or a Contains line.

check.q: A label says "May contain tree nuts." What does that mean?
choices: Tree nuts are a listed ingredient
The food could carry traces from shared equipment
check.why: An advisory statement warns of possible traces from shared lines; people with severe allergies should avoid it.

check.q: You have bought the same crackers for years. Do you still read the label?
choices: Yes, every time, because recipes change
Only if the box looks different
check.why: Companies change recipes without warning; check the label every purchase and before cooking.

review.q: Which is the correct order for a grease fire?
choices: Carry the pan outside, then call 911
Turn off the burner, slide on a lid, leave it until cool
Open a window, fan the flames, call 911
review.why: Heat off, smother with a lid, leave the lid on. Never water, never move the pan.
Pull the pin, aim at the base, squeeze the handle, sweep side to side.

review.q: Why is a sharp knife safer than a dull one?
choices: It needs less force, so it does not slip
review.why: A dull knife needs force and skids off food; a sharp one cuts where it is aimed.

review.q: Toast is stuck in a plugged-in toaster. What is the first step?
review.why: Always unplug before reaching into an appliance.

review.q: A burn on the wrist is red and blistered. What is the first treatment?
choices: Cool running water for at least ten minutes
review.why: Cool tap water stops the heat going deeper; never ice, butter or popping blisters.

review.q: Which of these is a major food allergen under U.S. law?
review.why: Sesame joined milk, eggs, fish, shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat and soy as the ninth major allergen.

review.q: A classmate is silent, grabbing his throat and cannot cough. What is right?
choices: Call 911 and give back blows and abdominal thrusts if trained
review.why: No cough, no speech and no breath means a blocked airway; act and call 911.

review.q: Fire is inside the oven. What should you do?
choices: Keep the door closed and turn the oven off
Open the door and pull out the dish
Pour baking soda through the door
Spray it with the sink hose
review.why: A closed oven starves the fire of air; opening the door feeds it.
